syllabusTopics: Limits and continuity: limits of a function, indeterminate forms, algebraic properties of limits (without proof), basic theorems on limits of algebraic, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions
Continuity of a function, types of discontinuity, graphs of discontinuous function
Derivatives: derivative of a function, derivatives of algebraic, trigonometric, inverse trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions by definition (simple forms)
Rules of differentiation; derivatives of parametric and implicit functions; higher order derivatives
Geometric interpretation of derivative; monotonicity of a function, interval of monotonicity, extreme values of a function, concavity, points of inflection
Anti-derivatives: integration using basic integrals, integration by substitution and by parts methods
The definite integral; the definite integral as an area under the given curve; area between two curves

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Monotonicity is read from the sign of the derivative across an interval, and extreme values come from where that sign changes. Solving $f'=0$ alone yields only candidates, as $x^3$ demonstrates. On a closed interval the endpoints are also candidates, and omitting them is the most common loss of marks in this topic.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Increasing: $f'(x)>0$; decreasing: $f'(x)<0$
Stationary: $f'(c)=0$
First-derivative test: $+\to-$ maximum, $-\to+$ minimum

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Treating every solution of $f'=0$ as a maximum or a minimum.  ·  Forgetting the two endpoints when finding absolute extrema on a closed interval.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Where a formula is quoted it is valid only under the conditions stated; Treating every solution of $f'=0$ as a maximum or a minimum.  ·  Every result here follows from the definitions, so a first-principles derivation is always a valid fallback in the exam.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: $f'=0$ gives candidates only; the SIGN CHANGE decides the extremum.  ·  Endpoints must be included when hunting absolute extrema on a closed interval.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Checking $f'$ at a single point instead of across the interval when deciding monotonicity.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Work through the authored practice problems and re-derive each key formula from the definition.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Build a sign chart for $f'$ across the critical points — the arrows give every classification at once.  ·  Write the endpoint values down explicitly before concluding on a closed interval.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Absolute extrema of a continuous function on a stated closed interval is a very frequent 4-mark question.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Topic anchor: Sign-change signature increasing then decreasing gives a maximum, decreasing then increasing gives a minimum.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Local and absolute extrema are different questions and both may be asked.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Fermat's principle of least time — light bending at an interface — follows directly from the stationary condition on travel time, tying this topic to optics.  ·  Any closed loop over hilly ground must have both a highest and a lowest point, which is the stationary-point condition in ordinary clothes.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Sign of $f'$ decides direction:** $f'>0$ means strictly increasing and $f'<0$ strictly decreasing over an INTERVAL. One negative value inside an increasing interval changes nothing, so the sign must be tested across the whole interval.  ·  **Stationary points are only candidates:** they are where $f'=0$, and a turning point is the subset where $f'$ actually CHANGES SIGN. $y=x^3$ has a stationary point at 0 with no extremum, because the sign of $3x^2$ is positive both sides — declaring a maximum straight from $f'=0$ is the commonest error here.  ·  **Fermat's theorem:** if $f$ is differentiable at an interior point $c$ and $f'(c)=0$, then $f(c)$ is a local extreme. The contrapositive is equally useful — an interior local extremum of a differentiable function must have vanishing derivative.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Absolute extrema on $[a,b]$: compare critical values with $f(a)$ and $f(b)$  ·  Fermat: $f'(c)=0$ at an interior local extremum, if differentiable  ·  Statement 1: $f$ is strictly increasing on an interval where $f'>0$ throughout.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Statement 2: $f'(c)=0$ is necessary but not sufficient for a local extremum.  ·  Statement 3: A sign change in $f'$ is required to classify a stationary point.  ·  Statement 4: A continuous function on $[a,b]$ attains an absolute maximum and minimum.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Statement 5: Fermat's theorem applies only to interior points of the domain.  ·  **Absolute extrema on a closed interval:** a continuous function on $[a,b]$ attains both. Check interior critical points FIRST, then the two ENDPOINTS — endpoints are frequently the true answer and are the most commonly forgotten candidates.  ·  **Local versus absolute:** a local maximum only beats its immediate neighbours, so a point can be a local minimum yet lie far above the absolute maximum elsewhere. Reading 'maximum' as 'absolute maximum' without a global check is a frequent conceptual slip.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Sign-change signature:** increasing then decreasing gives a maximum, decreasing then increasing gives a minimum. This is the first-derivative test, and it is why the sign chart rather than the equation $f'=0$ decides the answer.
